title: How To Find The Right Investors For Your Company
summary: Find startup investors by stage, sector, geography, and check size. Use a qualification worksheet and outreach templates to build a focused shortlist.
body_markdown:
## A copyable investor qualification worksheet


Use one row per prospect. Keep facts, open questions, and your judgment separate.


Field What to record What would change your decision?


Firm and person Organization, relevant partner or angel, and official profile link. The person no longer works there or covers a different mandate.


Stage and sector fit Current thesis plus one relevant investment or explicit focus statement. The investor excludes your stage, sector, or business model.


Geographic fit Published territory or an unanswered question to confirm. Your company falls outside the stated geography.


Check size and round role Published range, stated lead preference, or “not yet verified.” The likely commitment or role does not fit the round.


Relationship path Direct relationship, potential connector, or appropriate direct-contact route. The connector does not know them well enough to introduce you.


Source and date Links supporting the entry and when you last checked them. The evidence is stale, unclear, or contradicted by newer information.


Next action Research, request an introduction, contact directly, wait, or exclude. A reply, new mandate information, or a portfolio conflict changes the plan.


**Illustrative example:** A pre-seed climate-software startup finds a fund with a climate portfolio company. That is a promising lead, but the founder still needs to verify software focus, geography, and current check size. The worksheet keeps the prospect in “research” until those questions have answers.


## Prioritize fit before access


Give each prospect one of three simple statuses: **ready to contact** , **needs research** , or **not a fit** . A warm path to a mismatched investor should not outrank a well-supported fit with an appropriate direct-contact route.


For ready prospects, write a one-sentence rationale: “We are contacting this person because \[current evidence of fit\], and our next step is \[specific action\].” If the rationale is vague, do more research before sending.


## Make an introduction request easy to evaluate


Ask a connector whether they are comfortable introducing you. Give them enough context to decide, and make it easy to decline.


> Hi \[name\], I noticed you know \[investor\]. We are building \[plain-language company description\], and their focus on \[verified area\] looks relevant to our \[stage\] round. Do you know them well enough to consider an introduction? No problem if not. I can send a short forwardable note if helpful.


A direct message should be just as specific. Avoid implying that a mutual contact has endorsed you when they have not.


> Hi \[investor\], your work with \[relevant company or published thesis\] caught my attention. We help \[customer\] solve \[problem\], and have \[accurate evidence\]. We are preparing a \[stage\] round and would value a conversation if this fits your current mandate. Here is a brief overview: \[approved link\].


## Give the research an AI teammate


Assign Aurora a bounded job: prepare a sourced shortlist using your funding brief, identify missing information, and suggest the next research action. Keep the decision about fit and outreach with your team.


> Research startup investors for \[company and round\]. Use \[stage, sector, geography, and check-size criteria\]. Check existing records before proposing new prospects. Return firm, relevant person, fit evidence, source links, uncertainties, and a suggested next action. Do not send messages or assume introductions have been approved.

You can keep that work organized in[tools like Finta](https://finta.ai/login?intent=trial) , rather than letting the research live in disconnected tabs.


## Turn the shortlist into a fundraising process


Keep the list current as replies arrive. Record who owns the relationship, which materials were shared, what the investor asked for, and when you will act next. Learn from the conversations without treating silence as a precise measure of investor interest.
